title: GPIO: Digital and Analog I/O
subtitle: Pins, voltage levels, pull-up resistors, and ADC
author: Kernal Team

whyItExists.problem: Microcontrollers need to interact with the physical world: read button presses, detect sensor voltages, drive LEDs, control motors. Without understanding GPIO configuration, you get floating inputs (random readings), damaged pins, or non-functional circuits.
whyItExists.solution: GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output) pins are configurable as inputs or outputs. Understanding pull-up/pull-down resistors, voltage levels, ADC, and PWM lets you correctly interface any sensor or actuator.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every time you connect a physical component: buttons, LEDs, sensors, relays, displays, or any external hardware.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For high-speed digital interfaces (SD card, Ethernet), use dedicated hardware peripherals (SPI, I2C) rather than bit-banging GPIO.

explainModes.beginner: GPIO pins are like switches that you can control from code. You can set them as OUTPUT to light an LED, or INPUT to read a button. The tricky part is making sure input pins don't float around randomly — that's what pull-up resistors fix.
explainModes.simple: Each GPIO pin can be digital (0V or 5V) or analog (0-5V gradient). Set a pin as OUTPUT and write HIGH/LOW. Set it as INPUT and read its state. Add a pull-up resistor (or use the built-in one) so buttons read stable values.
explainModes.standard: GPIO pins are configured via the DDR (Data Direction Register) or pinMode(). Digital pins sample the input voltage against a threshold (typically 0.3*Vcc for LOW, 0.7*Vcc for HIGH). Analog pins feed a 10-bit SAR ADC producing values 0–1023. PWM uses hardware timers to generate variable-duty-cycle square waves.
explainModes.technical: On AVR, each port has three registers: DDRx (direction), PORTx (output/pull-up), PINx (input). Setting DDRx bit = 1 makes it output; PORTx bit = 1 enables the internal 20–50 kΩ pull-up when in input mode. The ADC has a 13-clock-cycle conversion time at 16 MHz = 9.6 kSPS max.
explainModes.deepDive: AVR GPIO sink/source current limits are 40 mA per pin and 200 mA per port. Exceeding these permanently damages the chip. The SAR ADC uses a successive-approximation algorithm and shares a multiplexer across all analog pins. PWM frequency on Timer0/2 is ~976 Hz; Timer1 is ~488 Hz with 8-bit resolution, or configurable up to 16-bit with ICR1.

content.text: GPIO pins are the bridge between your microcontroller and the physical world. Every pin can be configured as an output (drive voltage high or low) or input (read external voltage). Arduino Uno has 14 digital pins (D0–D13) and 6 analog pins (A0–A5) that also work as digital GPIO.
Digital Output: Driving LEDs and Relays

Always use a current-limiting resistor (220Ω–1kΩ) in series with an LED. Without it, the LED draws too much current and either burns out instantly or damages the GPIO pin. Formula: R = (Vcc - Vf) / If = (5V - 2V) / 20mA = 150Ω minimum.
Digital Input: Reading Buttons with Pull-Up

An unconnected (floating) input pin picks up electrical noise and reads random HIGH or LOW values. You need to bias it to a known state using a pull-up or pull-down resistor. Arduino has a convenient built-in INPUT_PULLUP mode that connects an internal ~50 kΩ resistor to Vcc.

Always use INPUT_PULLUP instead of INPUT when reading buttons. Floating inputs give random, unpredictable readings. The logic is inverted: LOW means pressed (button pulls pin to GND), HIGH means released.
Analog Input: Reading Sensors with ADC

Arduino's 10-bit ADC converts an analog voltage (0–5V) to a digital number (0–1023). Use analogRead(A0) to read pins A0–A5. This is essential for sensors that output a variable voltage: potentiometers, thermistors, light-dependent resistors (LDR), and soil moisture sensors.

PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) simulates analog output by rapidly switching a digital pin between HIGH and LOW at a fixed frequency. The duty cycle (percentage of time HIGH) controls the perceived voltage. analogWrite(pin, 0–255) sets the duty cycle on PWM-capable pins (marked ~ on Arduino Uno: 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11).

a.name: 5V Logic (Arduino Uno / Nano)
weaknesses: Requires level shifter for Raspberry Pi
a.useWhen: Using 5V sensors, traditional Arduino shields, or legacy components

b.name: 3.3V Logic (ESP32 / Raspberry Pi / Arduino Zero)
weaknesses: 5V on input will damage the chip permanently
b.useWhen: Modern sensors, WiFi/BT modules, Raspberry Pi GPIO

content.text: Never connect a 5V signal to a 3.3V GPIO pin (ESP32, Raspberry Pi, Arduino Zero/MKR). It will permanently damage the input protection diodes or the GPIO controller. Use a voltage divider (two resistors) or a dedicated logic-level converter IC.

questions.question: What does INPUT_PULLUP do?
options: Boosts the GPIO current output capability
Connects an internal ~50kΩ resistor to Vcc so unconnected pins read HIGH
Sets the pin as an analog output
questions.explanation: INPUT_PULLUP connects the internal pull-up resistor so the pin defaults to HIGH. When a button pulls it to GND, it reads LOW — logic is inverted compared to a pull-down configuration.

questions.question: What value does analogRead() return for a 2.5V input on a 5V Arduino?
questions.explanation: The 10-bit ADC maps 0–5V to 0–1023. 2.5V is half of 5V, so: 2.5 / 5.0 × 1023 ≈ 512.

questions.question: Which pins on Arduino Uno support analogWrite() (PWM)?
questions.explanation: PWM is generated by hardware timers. On the Uno, only pins 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, and 11 are timer-connected and support analogWrite() — these are marked with a ~ symbol on the board.

faq.q: Can I connect a 5V sensor to a Raspberry Pi GPIO?
faq.a: No! Raspberry Pi GPIO is 3.3V. A 5V signal will damage it. Use a voltage divider (10kΩ + 20kΩ resistors) or a dedicated bidirectional logic-level converter module.

faq.q: My LED is very dim even at full analogWrite(255). Why?
faq.a: Your resistor value may be too high, or the LED Vf (forward voltage) is higher than expected. Try a 220Ω resistor. Blue and white LEDs have ~3.2V Vf vs ~2V for red/green, so they're dimmer on 5V Arduino.

faq.q: Why does my button cause multiple triggers?
faq.a: Mechanical switch bounce — the contacts physically bounce on contact, generating multiple edges. Debounce in software with a 10–20 ms delay after first trigger, or use the Bounce2 library.

usedIn: Sensor voltage reading (thermistor, LDR, soil moisture)

Using analogRead(A0) to read a potentiometer and map it to servo position
